Canberra dementia summit faces cancellation over $52K shortfall

Nicholas Fuller
November 24, 2026
Facebook
Twitter
WhatsApp
    Email
    Copy URL
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:35
Instaread

Two months ago, dementia advocates announced an ACT Dementia Navigation Summit would be held in February to design a model for a dementia navigator – a much-needed specialist who could help people with dementia and their carers navigate an often bafflingly complex system.

But that summit could be cancelled unless organisers can raise $52,000 by mid-December, co-chair Greg Fraser has warned.

Organisers have launched a GoFundMe campaign to raise the sum by 18 December, and are looking for public donations so the summit can take place.

“I will be bitterly disappointed if we can’t make this summit happen,” Mr Fraser, former CEO of ACT Health and former director of Dementia Australia, said. “I’ve listened to a lot of people with dementia and a lot of their carers – and a lot of these people suffer greatly.

“It will be a tragedy for people with dementia and their carers because they will have to continue dealing with a system that does not take account of their needs. People with dementia will continue to not receive the care they need when and where they need it.”

Dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia, and the number of people living with dementia is expected to double in the next 30 years. An estimated 6,300 Canberrans live with dementia, projected to rise to 12,300 by 2054.

But health, disability and aged care systems are difficult to navigate and not serving patients’ and carers’ needs, Mr Fraser said.

This results in prolonged, avoidable hospitalisations; premature admission to residential aged care; duplication and inefficiency across government-funded services; unnecessary distress and decline for people with dementia; and carer burnout, co-chair Shelley Thomson’s research shows.

“It’s a major health, social and economic issue for the country,” Mr Fraser said. “If we can’t get the system working better, there are potentially going to be some disasters going forward.”

The two-day summit, intended to be held at the University of Canberra on 9 and 10 February, would bring together people with lived experience, clinicians, service providers and government to develop a model for a trained person connecting carers and patients with the right services at the right time. Navigators are already used in cancer care, and dementia navigator programs work overseas, Ms Thomson said. The model could be replicated elsewhere in Australia.

“This is one way to assist in getting the system working better for people with dementia and their carers – particularly for those people that have behavioural and psychological changes as a result of their dementia,” Mr Fraser said.

“They are the most difficult group of people to be placed in residential aged care. They make up a considerable population of the people occupying hospital beds for long periods of time.”

The $52,000 the organisers seek would help pay people with dementia and their carers to take part, so lived experience shapes the model; cover respite so carers can attend; bring interstate experts to Canberra; and run the summit and publish its report and roadmap.

The privately funded summit has already raised $65,200 from aged care providers, including its gold sponsor, Goodwin Aged Care; dementia organisations; community groups; the University of Canberra; and local businesses.

Mr Fraser has asked ACT health minister Dr Marisa Paterson whether the ACT Government could contribute $30,000, as the summit would benefit the Territory. Independent modelling for Dementia Australia found that every dollar invested in navigators would return about four, through fewer hospital stays and later entry to residential care, Ms Thomson said.

To donate to the GoFundMe campaign, visit https://www.gofundme.com/f/no-family-should-navigate-dementia-alone.
